blocks.text: A calendar MCP server wraps a real calendar service, like Google Calendar, so an AI agent can check schedules and create events on a person's behalf.
Instead of a human hunting for a free hour, the agent asks the server directly and gets a real answer back.
The tricky part is rarely the calendar logic itself. It is almost always timezones.
1. What This Server Wraps
Underneath, this server is a thin layer over a real calendar provider's API, most often Google Calendar or Microsoft Outlook.
That underlying API already knows about calendars, events, attendees, and a free busy endpoint for checking open time.
The MCP server's job is to expose a small, safe set of tools and resources on top of that existing API.

items: Calendar, a container that holds a set of events for one person or one team
Event, a single meeting with a start time, an end time, and a list of attendees
Attendee, a person invited to an event, each with their own timezone
Free busy, a lightweight view of when a calendar is open or occupied

blocks.text: 2. Tools This Server Needs
Two tools cover almost every real use case, one to check availability, and one to create an event.
A few servers add extras, like updating or canceling an event, but the core pair does most of the work.

items: check_availability, looks for open time across one or more calendars
create_event, books a new event with attendees, a time, and a timezone
update_event and cancel_event, optional tools for changes after the fact

blocks.text: 3. Tool: check_availability

blocks.alt: An AI agent talks to a calendar server which calls check_availability and create_event

blocks.text: This tool takes a time range and a list of calendars, and returns which parts of that range are free.
It should always ask for and return times with an explicit timezone, never a bare local time with no context.

code.content:
from zoneinfo import ZoneInfo
from datetime import datetime

def check_availability(calendar_ids, start_time, end_time, timezone):
    tz = ZoneInfo(timezone)
    start_utc = datetime.fromisoformat(start_time).replace(tzinfo=tz).astimezone(ZoneInfo("UTC"))
    end_utc = datetime.fromisoformat(end_time).replace(tzinfo=tz).astimezone(ZoneInfo("UTC"))

    freebusy = calendar_api.query_freebusy(
        calendar_ids=calendar_ids,
        time_min=start_utc.isoformat(),
        time_max=end_utc.isoformat(),
    )

    busy_blocks = merge_busy_ranges(freebusy)
    free_slots = subtract_busy_from_range(start_utc, end_utc, busy_blocks)
    return {"timezone": "UTC", "free_slots": free_slots}

blocks.text: Notice the tool converts to UTC before ever calling the calendar API, so busy blocks from different sources line up correctly.
4. Tool: create_event
This tool books a real event once the agent has picked a time, so it needs a title, a time range, a timezone, and attendees.
The safest design stores the event's start and end in UTC internally, while still showing the organizer's local time in the response.
The response converts back to the organizer's timezone purely for display, the stored value never changes.
5. Handling Timezones Correctly

blocks.alt: Two attendees in different timezones must resolve to the same moment in time

blocks.text: Timezones are the single most common source of calendar bugs, and MCP servers are no exception.
The safest rule is simple, store and compare everything in UTC, and only convert to a local timezone at the very last step, for display.

blocks.title: Never trust a bare timestamp
blocks.content: A time like 2026-07-09T14:00:00 with no timezone attached is ambiguous and dangerous. Always carry an explicit timezone name or offset alongside it.

blocks.text: Daylight saving time makes this worse, since the same local hour can mean a different UTC offset depending on the date.

items: Always require a timezone name, like America/New_York, alongside any local time the agent supplies
Convert to UTC immediately, before storing or comparing anything
Convert back to local time only when showing a result to a person
Use a real timezone database, like IANA tz data, never a fixed hour offset

blocks.text: 6. Comparing Times Across Calendars
Once every time is in UTC, comparing two people's busy blocks is just simple interval math.
Skip that conversion, and two calendars in different timezones will look free or busy at the wrong moments.
This overlap check only works because every value entering it was normalized to UTC first.
7. Resources: Exposing Upcoming Events
Alongside tools, this server can expose a resource that lists a person's upcoming events as read only context.
That lets the agent see what is already on the calendar without needing to call a tool just to look.
8. Resource URIs and Freshness
A resource URI like calendar colon slash slash primary slash events slash upcoming should return a snapshot, plus a note on how fresh it is.
Calendars change constantly, so the agent should treat a resource read from a minute ago as possibly stale.

blocks.text: 9. Finding a Slot for Multiple Attendees

blocks.alt: Free time from attendee A and attendee B overlaps into one open slot

blocks.text: The real value of this server shows up when an agent needs to schedule a meeting across several people's calendars at once.
The approach is to pull free busy data for every attendee, convert it all to UTC, and look for a shared open window.
10. Free Busy Data From the Provider

blocks.alt: The calendar provider returns free busy data for a given time range

blocks.text: Most calendar providers expose a dedicated free busy endpoint that is cheaper and faster than reading full event details.
It returns just busy time ranges per calendar, which is exactly what a slot finding tool needs.
This scan always works in UTC, so it does not matter that attendees sit in three different timezones.
11. Conflict Detection and Double Booking

blocks.alt: A new event overlapping an existing one is flagged as a double booking conflict

blocks.text: Before create_event actually books anything, a careful server rechecks availability one more time.
That guards against a race where someone else grabbed the slot between the check and the booking.

blocks.title: Recheck right before booking
blocks.content: A slot that was free a few seconds ago may not be free anymore. Always run one last availability check inside create_event before writing the event.

blocks.text: 12. Recurring Events and Edge Cases

blocks.alt: A recurring event series expands into individual occurrences with edge cases

blocks.text: Recurring events add real complexity, since a single series can have exceptions, like one instance moved or cancelled.
A safe server expands a recurring series into individual occurrences before checking busy time, rather than treating it as one block.
It also needs to handle an attendee declining just one instance, not the whole series.

items: Expand recurring series into individual occurrences before any free busy check
Treat a modified single instance as its own event, separate from the series
Watch for a series that crosses a daylight saving time change partway through
Never assume every occurrence in a series keeps the exact same UTC offset

blocks.text: 13. Authenticating with the Calendar Provider
This server needs an OAuth token scoped to calendar access, issued per user, never one shared account for everyone.
Tokens should be stored securely and refreshed automatically before they expire, not discovered as expired mid request.

items: calendar.readonly, enough for check_availability and reading resources
calendar.events, needed for create_event and any updates
Refresh tokens stored encrypted, never logged in plain text

blocks.text: 14. Error Handling for Calendar Operations
A declined invite, a deleted event, or a provider outage all need distinct, clear error responses.
The agent should be told plainly when a slot it picked got taken, so it can retry with a fresh check rather than guessing.

items: Slot no longer free, return a clear conflict error, not a generic failure
Attendee email invalid, fail before booking, not after
Provider API down, return a retryable error with a suggested wait

blocks.text: None of these errors should ever look like a plain success with an empty result.
15. Rate Limits and Caching

blocks.alt: Repeated calendar reads are cached to stay under the provider rate limit

blocks.text: Free busy lookups are cheap to call often, but calendar providers still enforce their own rate limits.
Caching an availability check for a short window, a few seconds, avoids hammering the provider when an agent checks the same range repeatedly.
Never cache create_event, booking must always hit the real provider.
Worked Example
An agent needs to schedule a thirty minute sync between three people in New York, London, and Tokyo.
First it calls check_availability for each attendee's calendar, converting every busy block to UTC.
Then it scans for a thirty minute UTC window where all three are free, using the same merge and scan logic as find_common_slot.
It finds one window at 14:00 UTC, and converts that back to each attendee's local time for display.
Finally it calls create_event with the UTC time and the organizer's timezone, and the invite reaches everyone at the correct local hour.

blocks.text: Common Mistakes

items: Storing or comparing local times without ever converting to UTC first
Assuming a fixed hour offset instead of using real timezone database rules
Forgetting that daylight saving time shifts the UTC offset on certain dates
Booking an event without a final availability recheck right before create_event
Treating a whole recurring series as one busy block instead of expanding occurrences
Returning a bare timestamp with no timezone attached in a tool response

blocks.text: Practice
Build a check_availability tool that accepts a timezone name, converts to UTC, and returns free slots for two calendars.
Then extend it to find_common_slot across three calendars in three different timezones, and print the result in each attendee's local time.
Key Takeaway
A calendar MCP server is mostly about two tools, check_availability and create_event, wrapped carefully around timezone safe logic.
Store and compare everything in UTC, convert to local time only for display, and always recheck availability right before booking.
